```{r, include = FALSE}
# A chunk's code sits under "Show code": open when it is what the page is
# about (`fold = "open"`), closed when it only supports it (`fold = "closed"`,
# the default unless the page sets another); `fold = FALSE` shows it plain,
# and so is code of three lines or fewer.
# Its results stay outside, always shown.
.fold_src <- knitr::knit_hooks$get("source")
knitr::knit_hooks$set(source = function(x, options) {
  f <- if (is.null(options$fold)) "closed" else options$fold
  # short code -- three lines or fewer, a chunk or the part of one before
  # its next output -- is shown as it is: folded, it would hide less than
  # the fold itself takes
  if (isFALSE(f) || length(unlist(strsplit(x, "\n", fixed = TRUE))) <= 3L) {
    return(.fold_src(x, options))
  }
  paste0("\n\n<details", if (identical(f, "open")) " open", ">",
         "<summary>Show code</summary>\n\n",
         .fold_src(x, options), "\n\n</details>\n\n")
})
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fold = "open")   # this page: the code is the subject
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE)
```

This article is for a contributor who works with an **agent**: a tool that
edits files and runs commands in the repository. Two such tools are covered:
the Claude desktop app (its Code tab) and VS Code with GitHub Copilot's
agent. This page gives what is the same for both. The steps for each tool are
on its own page:

* [Set-up in the Claude desktop app](ai-agents-claude-app.html)
* [Set-up in VS Code with GitHub Copilot](ai-agents-vscode-copilot.html)

Items marked **(to check)** are not confirmed yet. Treat them as open
questions, not as facts. Advice that is the article's own, and not from a tool's
documentation, is said to be so.

## 1. What this article is for

Some pages already cover nearby ground. This one does not repeat them.

* `CONTRIBUTING.md` and the [architecture article](architecture.html) give the
  rules: branches, labels, review, versioning.
* [Developing with an AI assistant](ai-development.html) is for a chat
  assistant that you give the AI developer manual.
* This article is about the set-up of an agent, how to work with it, and how to
  check what it made.

One set-up serves the three packages, rtfreporter, tflspec and tflplanner,
because one change often crosses them. Where a package differs, the text says
so.

Two things are outside this article: writing analysis code for a study (see
[Asking an AI chat for a table's plan code](ai-plan-code.html)), and the AI kits
that the packages ship for their users.

## 2. The environment

An agent installs branch builds and runs tests. If your own R library is on the
path, a test can pass only because of a package that you happen to have
installed. An install can also overwrite a package that you use for other work.
So give the agent a separate **work library** and a separate **work home**.

* **R version.** Read it from `DESCRIPTION` (`Depends:`) and from the CI
  matrix in `.github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml`. Do not copy it from this page.
* **Folders.** Before the first R call, set `R_LIBS_USER`, `HOME` and the
  `R_USER_*` folders (`R_USER_CACHE_DIR`, `R_USER_DATA_DIR`,
  `R_USER_CONFIG_DIR`) to folders of the work area. This holds for a one-line
  `Rscript -e` call too. Set `TMP`, `TEMP` and `TMPDIR` as well, so that no
  file lands in the system temporary folder.
* **Windows.** Setting `HOME` alone is not enough: R still finds the user
  library. Set `R_LIBS_USER` too.
* **Which R.** Call the R that the project names, by its full path. Do not use
  whichever `Rscript` comes first on the path.

Run the script below first in every session. It prints the facts that matter
and stops if a library or folder outside the work area is in use. Set `WORK_ROOT` to the work
folder before you run it. The page shows the script and does not run it.

```{r check-env, eval = FALSE}
# check-env.R -- run first: Rscript check-env.R
# WORK_ROOT is the folder that holds the work library and the work home.
win <- .Platform$OS.type == "windows"
norm <- function(path) {
  p <- sub("/+$", "", normalizePath(path, winslash = "/", mustWork = FALSE))
  if (win) tolower(p) else p   # drive and folder case do not matter on Windows
}
root <- Sys.getenv("WORK_ROOT")
if (!nzchar(root) || !dir.exists(root)) {
  stop("Set WORK_ROOT to an existing work folder first.", call. = FALSE)
}
root <- norm(root)
# TRUE for the root itself and for a path below it; "C:/work-old" is not.
under_root <- function(path) {
  p <- norm(path)
  nzchar(path) && (p == root || startsWith(p, paste0(root, "/")))
}

cat("R:", R.version.string, "\n")
cat("R home:", R.home(), "\n")
cat("Library paths:\n")
print(.libPaths())

for (pkg in c("rtfreporter", "tflspec", "tflplanner")) {
  loc <- system.file(package = pkg)
  cat(sprintf("%-12s %s\n", pkg, if (nzchar(loc)) loc else "(not installed)"))
}
for (pkg in c("testthat", "lintr", "roxygen2", "covr")) {
  ver <- tryCatch(as.character(utils::packageVersion(pkg)),
                  error = function(e) "(not installed)")
  cat(sprintf("%-12s %s\n", pkg, ver))
}

# The base library and the site library of this R are allowed and listed;
# every other library must be in WORK_ROOT.
allowed <- unique(c(.Library, .Library.site))
cat("Allowed (base and site):\n", paste0("  ", allowed, collapse = "\n"), "\n")
libs <- .libPaths()
libs <- libs[!norm(libs) %in% norm(allowed)]
outside <- libs[!vapply(libs, under_root, logical(1))]

# R_LIBS_USER must be set, and each folder in it must exist and be in WORK_ROOT.
# (.libPaths() leaves out a folder that does not exist.)
user_libs <- strsplit(Sys.getenv("R_LIBS_USER"), .Platform$path.sep)[[1]]
bad_user <- length(user_libs) == 0L ||
  !all(vapply(user_libs, function(p) under_root(p) && dir.exists(p), logical(1)))

dirs <- Sys.getenv(c("HOME", "R_USER_CACHE_DIR", "R_USER_DATA_DIR",
                     "R_USER_CONFIG_DIR", "TMP", "TEMP", "TMPDIR"))
bad_dirs <- names(dirs)[!vapply(dirs, under_root, logical(1))]

if (length(outside) > 0L || bad_user || length(bad_dirs) > 0L) {
  if (length(outside) > 0L) {
    cat("Libraries outside WORK_ROOT:\n", paste0("  ", outside, collapse = "\n"), "\n")
  }
  if (bad_user) {
    cat("R_LIBS_USER is unset, missing, or outside WORK_ROOT.\n")
  }
  if (length(bad_dirs) > 0L) {
    cat("Folders outside WORK_ROOT (or unset):", paste(bad_dirs, collapse = ", "), "\n")
  }
  stop("A library or folder outside the work area is in use. Fix the environment first.",
       call. = FALSE)
}
cat("Environment OK.\n")
```

**Data.** Use fictional data only (Example Pharma) and the sample studies that
the packages ship. Never put company, study or patient data in code, tests,
issues, pull requests or an agent's session.

## 3. What the harness holds

The **harness** is everything around the agent: its instructions, its reusable
tasks, its permissions and the checks that decide.

### Instruction files

Keep one source and short pointers to it, not three copies. The files are:

* `AGENTS.md`: the shared orientation. This repository has one.
* `CLAUDE.md`: read by Claude Code. This repository has one. It imports
  `@AGENTS.md` and adds the notes for Claude Code. Keep it that way.
* `.github/copilot-instructions.md`: read by Copilot. This repository has one.

What they say should be short:

* where the authoritative documents are (`CONTRIBUTING.md`, the architecture
  article, the AI developer manual);
* which branch to work from;
* what an agent must not touch: `Version:` in `DESCRIPTION`, and `NEWS.md`;
* the test and lint commands;
* when to stop and ask.

Claude Code reads `CLAUDE.md` at the start of each session. It reads
`AGENTS.md` only when there is no `CLAUDE.md`, so a `CLAUDE.md` that wants the
shared text imports it, as this repository's does. Copilot in VS Code reads
`.github/copilot-instructions.md` or `AGENTS.md`. Each set-up page shows how to
confirm that the file was read. An instruction file is a request, not a lock:
Claude Code's documentation says so, and says that a hook is what blocks an
action.

### The pre-PR check as a reusable task

Both tools can keep a task that you start by name. The list is the same, so
either tool makes the same check. It is a faster subset, to run on each change:

1. Run the tests of the changed area.
2. Run `lintr::lint_package()`. The result must be 0 lints.
3. Check that every new `pkg::` use or `requireNamespace()` call is declared in
   `DESCRIPTION`.
4. When a change in tflspec can break tflplanner, run tflplanner's tests too.
5. Report each result in the PR description.

This task is not the four pre-push checks of `CONTRIBUTING.md`:
`R CMD check --as-cran`, `devtools::test()`, `pkgdown::check_pkgdown()` and
lintr. CI runs the full set, and so does a maintainer before a release.

The Claude desktop app holds the task as a **skill**, and VS Code as a
**prompt file**. The set-up pages show both.

### Checks that decide

An agent's judgment is not a check. These are:

* `testthat`, run as in `CONTRIBUTING.md`;
* `lintr`, with the repository's `.lintr`;
* `R CMD check`, and the `cran-readiness` workflow (spelling, URLs, example
  timings);
* coverage, in `test-coverage.yaml`;
* undeclared dependencies: search the diff for `pkg::` and
  `requireNamespace()` and compare the names with `DESCRIPTION`. **(To check:**
  whether a ready-made tool should replace this search.**)**
* a scan of the dependencies for known vulnerabilities. GitHub's list of
  ecosystems that Dependabot supports has GitHub Actions and has no row for R,
  so Dependabot does not read an R package's `DESCRIPTION`. This repository has
  no `.github/dependabot.yml` file today. **(To check:** which scanner to use for
  R dependencies, and what the repository settings already turn on.**)**

### Checks on each edit

Some rules are better enforced at each edit than at the end: lint a changed R
file, or refuse an edit to `Version:` in `DESCRIPTION` or to `NEWS.md`. Claude
Code does this with **hooks**. VS Code has hooks too, in Preview. The Claude
page shows an example set, which is in pull request #935 and not yet on the
default branch. The VS Code page shows the format of a hook. Where a tool cannot do it, the pre-PR check
and CI cover the same ground.

## 4. The workflow

### The loop

Issue, branch, small pull request, CI, review, merge.

* One change per pull request, with `Closes #n` in its description.
* A contributor opens the pull request against `main`. A maintainer's topic
  branch goes to `next`, which is merged to `main` about once a week
  (*Branching & collaboration* in `CONTRIBUTING.md`). `AGENTS.md`, which
  Copilot's instructions point to, names `main` only, so a maintainer who uses
  Copilot follows `CONTRIBUTING.md`.
* The description holds the *User-visible change (for NEWS)* text. The agent
  does not edit `NEWS.md` or the version.
* The agent opens the pull request. It does not merge it. The pause for review
  is the point.

### Test first

Ask the agent to write the test that fails before the fix, and to show it
failing. Then it fixes the code. For a bug report, the reproduction comes first
and goes into the issue or the pull request.

### What an agent does well

* Reproducing a problem and narrowing down its cause.
* A mechanical edit across many files.
* Writing tests.
* Translating text under a rule that you state.
* Bringing a branch up to date with `next`.

### What a person must check

Whatever the agent reports:

* **The numbers in an output.** Compare them with a count made another way
  (section 5).
* **Screens.** Look at them in a real browser.
* **Design decisions, API names, and anything users see.**
* **The next package.** A change in one package must not break the one after
  it (rtfreporter, tflspec, tflplanner).
* **That "done" matches the commit.** Read the diff, not the summary.

## 5. Checking the finished material

A table that looks right can still be wrong. The check is a comparison with
numbers that you worked out without the package.

### Hand-worked expected tables

Make a small fictional dataset (Example Pharma). Work out every count, percent
and N by hand, once, and keep the result next to the test. The test compares the
generated table with that result, cell by cell. It does not compare it with the
code's own earlier output.

### An example: blank values

Data read from a `.xpt` file gives a missing character value as `""`, not `NA`.
A table that counts causes then treats `""` as a category. It prints an extra
blank row, and its percents look right.

A test on in-memory data with `NA` passes and hides this. The hand-worked table,
made from data that was written and read back as the study stores it, catches
it.

### The order

1. Take the data as the study stores it (write it to `.xpt` and read it back).
2. Make the expected table by hand.
3. Run the package.
4. Compare the two, cell by cell.
5. Then a person looks at the page.

When a check has found a problem once, keep it as a regression test.

## 6. The two tools, feature by feature

| Job | Claude desktop app (Code tab) | VS Code with Copilot |
|---|---|---|
| Standing instructions for the repository | `CLAUDE.md`. `AGENTS.md` is read only when there is no `CLAUDE.md`, unless `CLAUDE.md` imports it. | `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, or `AGENTS.md`. |
| A reusable task (the pre-PR check) | A skill: `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, started with `/name`. | A prompt file: `.github/prompts/<name>.prompt.md`, started with `/name`. |
| Running tests and lint | Runs commands in a terminal tool. | Runs commands in the integrated terminal. |
| What it may run without asking | Permission rules and permission modes. | Terminal auto-approve rules (`chat.tools.terminal.autoApprove`). |
| Checks on each edit | Hooks in `.claude/settings.json`. | Hooks (Preview) in `.github/hooks/*.json`. |
| Handing a piece of work to a helper | Separate sessions; each can use its own worktree. | Subagents, which work in their own context. |
| Reading an Issue or a pull request | `gh` in the terminal. The app shows a pull request's CI status after you open it. | **(To check:** how Copilot in VS Code reads an Issue or a pull request.**)** |

The facts in this table come from the tools' own documentation, read on
2026-11-08; the set-up pages link the pages. Tools change fast, so check the
tool's documentation when a step does not work as written.
